topic: Getting more enquiries from Google without ads
title: How can a tradesman get more enquiries from Google without paying for ads?
metaTitle: Get More Enquiries From Google, Free
description: A practical guide for tradespeople: the free things that get your phone ringing from Google searches - profile, reviews, service pages and speed.
card: The free, practical steps that put your firm in front of people searching Google for a tradesperson in your area.
summary: Most free enquiries from Google come from three places: your Google Business Profile in the map results, the reviews on it, and a fast website with a page for each service and town you cover. Get those right, make it easy to call or message you, and reply quickly. It builds over weeks and months rather than overnight, but it keeps working without a monthly ad bill.

sections.heading: Where free enquiries from Google actually come from
paragraphs: When someone searches for a roofer, driveway firm or builder near them, Google shows a few different things. At the top there are usually ads. Below those is a map with a short list of local firms. Below that are ordinary website results.

You don't pay for the map or the website results. Both are free to appear in, but each has its own rules. The map list is driven by your Google Business Profile and your reviews. The website results are driven by how clearly your site shows what you do and where you do it, and how well it works on a phone.
So the job splits into two: get the profile right, and get the website right. Everything else in this guide supports one of those two.

sections.heading: Start with your Google Business Profile
paragraphs: For most local trades, this is the quickest win. It's the listing that shows your name, phone number, reviews and photos in the map results. If it's unclaimed, half-filled or out of date, you're handing those enquiries to someone else.
We cover the setup in full in our guide to a [Google Business Profile for tradesmen](/guides/google-business-profile-for-tradesmen). The essentials are below.

bullets.text: If you fit roofing, choose roofing, not something vague like general contractor. Add extra categories only for work you really do.
Write each one out in plain words, such as flat roof repairs, resin driveways or loft conversions.
List the towns you will actually travel to, not the whole county.
Finished jobs, your van, you at work. Genuine photos of your own work beat stock images.
Name, phone number and website should match your site and any directories exactly.

sections.heading: Collect reviews steadily
paragraphs: Reviews are what make someone pick you from the list. A firm with plenty of recent, specific reviews looks safer than one with a handful from years ago, even if the work is the same.

The habit that works is asking every happy customer at the end of every job, while they're still pleased with the result. Send them a direct link so it takes seconds. Our guide on [how to get more Google reviews](/guides/how-to-get-more-google-reviews) goes through the wording and timing.
Reply to every review, including the bad ones. A calm, factual reply to a complaint tells future customers more about you than the complaint itself does.

sections.heading: Give each service and town its own page
paragraphs: A common mistake is putting everything on one page: roofing, guttering, fascias, chimney repairs, all in one block, with a list of twenty towns at the bottom. Google can't tell what the page is really about, and a customer can't quickly find what they need.

A better set-up is one clear page per main service, and a page that makes plain where you work. Each page should say what you do, show a few real jobs of that type, mention the areas you cover and make it obvious how to get in touch.

Write it the way you'd explain the job to a customer on the phone. Avoid copying text from other firms or filling the page with the same phrase over and over. Plain, specific writing reads better and ranks better.

If you're a roofer, our guide on [what a roofer's website should include](/guides/website-design-for-roofers-what-it-needs) lists the pages and details to cover. Other trades can follow the same idea, and the [pages for specific trades](/websites-for/roofers) show how it applies.

sections.heading: Make the site fast on a phone
paragraphs: Most people searching for a tradesperson are on a phone, often in a hurry because something has gone wrong. If your page takes ages to appear, they go back and tap the next result. That costs you the enquiry, and it also tells Google people weren't happy with the page.

Heavy photos, page-builder code and too many add-ons are the usual causes. Compress your images before uploading them, remove anything you don't use, and test the site on your own phone using mobile data, not your home wifi.

You can check yours with the [free website speed test](/speed-test). It runs Google's own test and takes seconds. If the mobile result is poor, fixing that is often worth more than adding new content.

sections.heading: Make it easy to get in touch
paragraphs: Getting someone to your site is only half of it. If they have to hunt for a phone number or fill in a long form, many won't bother.

Put a tap-to-call button where a thumb can reach it on every page. Add WhatsApp if you're happy taking enquiries that way, and keep the contact form short: name, number and what they need. Every extra field loses a few people.

Then reply fast. Someone who has sent three enquiries to three firms will often go with whoever answers first. Set your phone to alert you when a form comes in, and give a quick holding reply even if you can't quote straight away.

sections.heading: Use directories as a supplement, not a replacement
paragraphs: Listings on sites like Checkatrade can bring work and can help people trust you. But you're renting that audience, and your listing sits alongside your competitors'. Your own site and your Google profile are things you control.
If you're weighing it up, read [Checkatrade or your own website](/guides/checkatrade-or-your-own-website). For many firms the answer is both, with your own site doing the long-term work.

sections.heading: Show your finished jobs
paragraphs: Every completed job is useful content. A short write-up with a few photos, the type of work, the town and what the customer wanted gives Google something specific to match against local searches. It also gives a customer proof that you do what you say.

You don't need to write an essay. A few sentences and good photos are enough. Add them to your site and post a matching update to your Google profile. Done regularly, this builds up a body of local evidence that a thin site never has.

sections.heading: What to expect, and what to check if nothing happens
paragraphs: Free search work is slower than ads. Ads stop the moment you stop paying, but they start at once. Organic enquiries usually build over weeks and months as your profile fills out, reviews accumulate and your pages get picked up. Don't expect an overnight change.

If you've done the basics and still hear nothing, work through our guide on a [website not getting enquiries](/guides/website-not-getting-enquiries). The usual culprits are a slow site, vague pages, a hard-to-find phone number or a half-finished profile.

faqs.q: Do I need a website if I have a Google Business Profile?
faqs.a: A profile can bring calls on its own, but a website gives you more to show and more places to be found. It also gives customers somewhere to check your work before they ring.

faqs.q: How long does it take to get more enquiries from Google?
faqs.a: It varies, but expect weeks to months rather than days. Tidying your profile and asking for reviews can show results sooner than new website pages do.

faqs.q: Is it worth paying for ads as well?
faqs.a: It can be, if you have a busy gap to fill quickly. But free search work lasts and compounds, so it's worth getting the profile, reviews and site right first.

faqs.q: Do I need to write a page for every town I cover?
faqs.a: No. Only cover areas you genuinely work in, and give each page real content such as local jobs. Thin pages that only swap the town name don't help you.

faqs.q: How do I know if my website is too slow?
faqs.a: Run it through the free speed test on this site and look at the mobile result. Also load it on your own phone using mobile data. If it feels slow to you, it feels slower to a customer.
